We analyze a collection of differential equation-based models, including compartmental frameworks such as SIR, SIRS, and SEIR, alongside a selected range of dynamic and machine learning approaches. Our analysis highlights the strengths and limitations of each model, with a specific focus on how these methods were applied to the COVID-19 crisis in Iran. We conclude by offering suggestions for future research directions. This work is grounded in the premise that appropriate mathematical modeling serves as a vital instrument for comprehending outbreak dynamics and informing effective management strategies. Differential equation models remain a primary approach in this domain, characterized by their capacity to balance mathematical complexity with computational efficiency and their ability to align theoretical predictions with empirical data. Dynamic models are essential not only for elucidating the mechanisms driving outbreaks but also for evaluating potential interventions. Ultimately, developing accurate models that yield reliable predictions is paramount for formulating effective policies to mitigate the adverse impacts of epidemics. Machine learning techniques have recently emerged as a promising alternative to dynamic models, particularly in estimating key parameters and making predictions during high-profile outbreaks. However, these methods often function as statistical tools lacking the explanatory power inherent in dynamic modeling frameworks. Consequently, integrating the predictive accuracy of machine learning with the mechanistic clarity of dynamic models represents a promising avenue for future inquiry.

We demonstrate that, under certain conditions, a three-body recombination process emerges as the primary loss mechanism, transforming all components into molecules. Our objective is to define a space-time coding framework suitable for all DNA-storage systems and utilize it to present two specific BarCode-space-time codes. The first system achieves constant space complexity, while the second offers constant time complexity; notably, both maintain a linear rate with regard to the message length. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to construct an $s$-th order BarCode-space-time code with a $\Theta(n^{1-1/s})$ rate, where $n$ represents the message length. Crucially, our most significant contribution is the first DNA-storage system design with a constant rate. To achieve this, we propose a straightforward single-barcode format and an advanced multi-barcode format that incorporates error correction. Our system operates within the constraints of modern DNA technology, requiring only $3000$ bases for single-barcode encoding and $60000$ bases for multi-barcode encoding. We validate the feasibility of our approach by successfully storing and retrieving test images using both barcode formats. The underlying algorithm is implemented in Python and accessible at \url{https://github.com/NoamBaruch/DNA-Storage}. Barcodes generated by our system can also be downloaded from \url{https://drive.google.com/drive/u/0/folders/15555555555555555555555555555555}. These single-barcode and multi-barcode formats are compatible with a Lysozyme-based NANO-array network, as detailed in [1]. To our knowledge, this marks the inaugural demonstration of using DNA barcodes for image storage in a NANO-array network. Our method utilizes DNA molecules as both memory units and addressing mechanism, thereby eliminating the need for PCR amplification or DNA sequencing. By employing 2D barcodes, our system bypasses the limitations imposed by DNA replication and reading lengths, which typically constrain existing DNA memory systems to low data rates. Additionally, our scheme avoids the costly optical 3D addressing required by other approaches. We anticipate that this work will facilitate the deployment of practical DNA memory systems.

a critical challenge in hydrological modeling. This study employs a physics-based numerical method to simulate velocity fields across various cross-sections of the Moselle river at different times and locations. These simulated velocities are then integrated into a machine learning framework that also utilizes key hydrological indicators, such as water level and discharge, to forecast flow speed at specific cross-sections. The study's primary objective is to demonstrate that flow velocity at a given cross-section can be predicted with high precision using only the water level at that location, a finding with significant implications for both scientific research and practical applications. Furthermore, the predicted velocities were employed to calibrate a nowcasting model designed to estimate water level changes at unmeasured cross-sections along the river. This model leverages the relationship between water level and flow velocity, utilizing the latter's accurate predictions to improve nowcasting performance. The research highlights the potential of accurate velocity prediction for enhancing cross-section water level predictions, thereby offering a robust solution for anticipating flood risks. The methodology and code are available on GitHub.

Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) preconditioners applied to a linearized fully coupled atmosphere-ocean model. The models were simulated on configurations corresponding to the CO2 doubling and pre-industrial climate scenarios. Experiments were conducted on parallel supercomputers utilizing grids with varying resolutions and physical time steps. Results indicate that for fine grids and large time steps, BDDC demonstrates a superior parallel performance relative to traditional AMG preconditioners. Specifically, BDDC exhibits a nearly constant number of preconditioner iterations across all tested problems, whereas traditional AMG shows an increasing number of iterations as the problem size grows. Furthermore, the study highlights that both BDDC and AMG preconditioners require more operations per iteration for the coupled atmosphere-ocean system compared to decoupled models. This increase is partly attributed to the higher cost of solving implicit Rostager-Propogation (RP) schemes in the ocean component when initialized with large atmospheric tracers errors. Consequently, the authors suggest that the perceived increase in FLOPS per physical time step for coupled models might partly stem from a rise in floating-point operations per RP iteration rather than a rise per physical time step. Additionally, the research examines the impact of the interface polynomial degree on BDDC performance and shows that even a low degree of one results in a near-optimal iteration count. Finally, the study analyzes the behavior of BDDC iterations at high latitudes during the winter season and compares these findings with those from traditional AMG preconditioners. Overall, these results suggest that the increased computational cost per iteration of BDDC and AMG preconditioners in polar regions arises from the discretization of the physical domain, not from the complexity of the underlying equations. This is evidenced by the fact that similar increases in preconditioner operations per iteration occur in other scalar field problems, such as surface pressure and total heat content. The number of BDDC iterations remains almost constant regardless of the time step size, although a larger time step leads to more oscillations in the residual. The authors conclude that, particularly for very fine grids and large time steps, BDDC and AMG preconditioners achieve similar performance levels. Notably, this represents a significant improvement over traditional AMG methods, which suffer from a rising iteration count and a lack of scalability on parallel architectures when solving the fully coupled linearized model. It is important to note that this analysis pertains to the linearity phase of the operational coupled model; therefore, further investigation is required to determine the performance of these preconditioners

distribution with variance growing linearly over time, is often considered the simplest form of spatial expansion. Nevertheless, in numerous physical, biological, and social contexts, Gaussian diffusion fails to adequately describe observed dynamics due to the influence of non-local interactions, external forces, boundaries, and other factors. This paper introduces a continuum model featuring a non-local, integral-advection term alongside a local, diffusive term. We demonstrate that this system admits a transformation into a coupled system of two integral equations, which we analyze to derive analytical insights regarding asymptotic behavioral dynamics. Specifically, we examine how the integral-advection term impacts the asymptotic distribution, revealing conditions under which the distribution remains Gaussian with a super-linearly growing variance or, conversely, becomes non-diffusive and localized. When the advection term is absent, the distribution is strictly Gaussian, with variance growth linear in time. Furthermore, we establish that the most aggressive advection term considered here cannot be balanced by any quadratic non-linearity in the density within the advection component to produce localized distributions; such a non-linearity merely reduces the rate of variance growth from linear to sub-linear. These findings are directly applicable to similar models where the integral term represents an irreversibly orienting force, such as phototaxis or chemotaxis. Additionally, we provide an overview of related models and summarize key open questions in this field.

This approach elucidates the origin of the Chern number, expressed via the Berry connection defined on the parameter space of the Hamiltonian. This Berry connection corresponds to a connection on a vector bundle constructed from the Hamiltonian's eigenspaces. In a typical Berry phase calculation, an external quantum particle traverses the parameter space, inducing an "Aharonov-Bohm" effect within the particle's eigenspace. Conversely, one can consider the particle at the center of space, enabling its eigenspace to connect with the space surrounding it through the quantum particle, thereby "pulling" a trajectory through the parameter space. This perspective offers a novel method for measuring the quantum Hall effect, the topological invariant of quantum spin Hall systems, and other quantum field theory invariants, such as those in $\mathbb{C}P^{N}$. The proposed framework provides a fresh viewpoint on quantum mechanics and topology, potentially yielding insights into unresolved issues in quantum field theory and string theory. Illustrative examples include the Chern number of the Landau level, the topological invariant of the Haldane model, 't Hooft-Polyakov monopoles, Grassmanian sigma models, and $SU(N)$ principal bundles. Notably, recent quantum information theory has already utilized a similar mechanism to define and quantify topological entanglement entropy. The quantum particle approach to computing Chern numbers is straightforward to implement and experimentally realize using a single quantum particle, as it avoids the challenges associated with adiabatically transporting an external particle through parameter space in a quantum system, which often involves unobservable electronic or photonic states. The quantum particle method is particularly advantageous for calculating Chern numbers on closed manifolds, which are essential for characterizing topological insulators. While numerical methods exist to compute intrinsic quantum numbers from Hamiltonian eigenvalues and eigenvectors, our quantum particle technique provides a direct observation of the quantum particle's response to topology, making the Chern number directly measurable. Although the quantum particle approach to Chern numbers was previously demonstrated by Shapourian et al. (arXiv:1509.05443), their work focused on a specific eigenspace (typically the ground state) and a straight-line trajectory in parameter space, yielding a curvature formula equivalent to the Fock-Schwinger field strength tensor in quantum field theory. In contrast, our paper develops a comprehensive and general theory of the Chern number, including its quantum particle formulation, across various mathematical settings

We introduce a framework that leverages Lifelog data to train models for specific activities. This approach utilizes a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to generate dense, semantic states from discrete, low-frequency events found in such logs. These states are then employed to train RL agents for goal-oriented goals using only video clips. The results demonstrate that using event-based dense states derived from lifelog videos yields a substantial performance boost when RL training is limited to short video segments compared to using frequent states. Recommender systems (RS) are increasingly deployed in high-profile sectors like healthcare and education. However, these systems often process data in isolation, failing to leverage the rich, multi-modal information available in lifelog data. This paper presents a two-stage framework for activity recognition in lifelogs that integrates semantic recommendations. Initially, an activity recommendation model uses video clips to predict dense states, which are then converted into a sequence of state-of-the-art lifelog representations for a first-stage activity recognizer. Subsequently, an activity-based recommendation model predicts life events from these state sequences for a second-stage recognizer. We evaluated an implementation of this framework across two distinct lifelog modalities—video and audio—and an image dataset. The results show that integrating semantic recommendations into activity recognition leads to performance gains, particularly when data is scarce. The code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/soheihara/Activity-with-SR-from-LifeLog.

While formal verification methods can ensure that recorded processes meet specific constraints, these approaches rely on predefined process models, which are not always available. This paper introduces a systematic framework for discovering data-aware process models from event logs. The discovery process begins by ensuring that alpha-mining algorithms capture both control flow and data dependencies. Although we focus on combining event log and assertion information, our framework is adaptable to other scenarios, such as tracing activity assertions in black-box systems. The study focuses on paired English-Greek datasets and investigates various sentiment classification approaches using multilingual representations from BERT and XLM-R. Results indicate that cross-lingual sentiment analysis yields superior outcomes compared to cross-lingual TF-IDF representations for both BERT and XLM-R models. Multilingual Natural Language Processing (NLP) has recently advanced significantly with the release of large-scale multilingual models like M3E and XLM-R. However, the effectiveness of these models in specific tasks remains uncertain. This study evaluates the performance of BERT and XLM-R on a Greek sentiment analysis dataset, assessing both in-language and cross-lingual configurations. Our findings reveal that for related languages, high-performance cross-lingual classifiers can be trained using only the target language's related high-resource representations. Additionally, we observe that corpus size and class imbalance heavily influence the feasibility of NLP tasks in low-resource languages. The released data and code will support future research in low-resource NLP.

Document coreference resolution (DCR) is essential for understanding texts, yet it remains challenging due to coreference variability and the high cost of creating manually annotated data. This paper presents a linguistic analysis of a new Italian DCR dataset, exploring coreference patterns across different text genres and sentence types. Our analysis highlights that DCR difficulty fluctuates based on the language variety and that certain entities are more likely to be coreferenced across Italian dialects than across standard Italian. These insights underscore the necessity of including diverse linguistic varieties in evaluation datasets. The Italian DCR dataset is accessible at https://github.com/robertolucare

the presence of pulmonary edema, a condition where fluid accumulates in the lungs. However, there has been a lack of quantitative studies assessing whether radiologists can identify patients with pulmonary edema using only X-rays, especially considering that edema can manifest in various patterns and levels of severity. This study presents a novel, clinically relevant framework for categorizing pulmonary edema into six distinct X-ray appearances. We collected over 1,000 X-ray pairs (1,600 images) of patients with and without pulmonary edema, annotated by three expert radiologists. Our analysis reveals that radiologists can differentiate patients with pulmonary edema from those without, achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.76 (95% CI: 0.71–0.81) in a cross-patient study. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these X-ray appearances are not simply variations in brightness or contrast, as masking regions labeled as pulmonary edema minimally impacts the ability to detect the condition. In conclusion, we introduce a new taxonomy for pulmonary edema and provide evidence that radiologists can discern its presence and specific appearance from X-rays, despite the challenge posed by the condition's diverse manifestations. This taxonomy can aid clinicians in describing and recognizing pulmonary edema patterns, potentially enhancing communication and collaboration among healthcare providers. Additionally, the annotated dataset is available to facilitate future research into the characterization and prediction of pulmonary edema using X-rays. Our findings also suggest that appearance-based explanations should be considered when training deep learning models to detect pulmonary edema. To our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate that pulmonary edema has distinct X-ray appearances and that radiologists can identify patients with the condition based on these appearances.

We present a method for automatically annotating the temporal progression of COVID-19 in radiology reports. By analyzing reports from 1,085 patients, we identified six key phases: infection, consolidation, resorption, scar tissue, recurrent infection, and recurrence of scar tissue. These phases were extracted using a combination of natural language processing and expert validation. We developed a deep learning model to classify radiology reports based on these annotations and trained it on a dataset where each report was labeled with the earliest phase present. This paper investigates the algebraic structures known as $W$-modules. We establish that every $G$-bundle arises from a specific descent condition linked to a naturally defined transformation between the functor of points of $\mathcal{C}$ and the functor of points represented by the total space of the universal bundle over $\mathcal{C}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the group of morphisms from $W(G)$ to $W(H)$ in the category of $W$-modules corresponds precisely to the group of $H$-equivariant maps from $G$ to $H$. Finally, we show that the category of $W$-modules is equivalent to the category of group objects within the Eilenberg-Moore category of the monad $G \mapsto WG$. These findings provide a novel characterization of this equivalence and reveal that the forgetful functor from $W$-modules to simplicial groups preserves limits. Additionally, we derive a characterization of the Barr-exactness of the category of groups based on the adjunction between simplicial groups and simplicial sets. Along the way, we characterize the unit of the comonad induced by $W$ on $sGrp(\mathcal{C})$ and provide a new description of the group of morphisms $[W(G), H]$ for any simplicial set $H$. These results hold significance in homotopy theory, particularly regarding the equivalence between the homotopy categories of simplicial groups and $K(\cdot,1)$-spaces. The characterization of $[WG, H]$ extends naturally to the setting of Segal spaces, yielding a corresponding result for the category of $W$-modules within that context. This generalization also offers a new proof of the equivalence between the homotopy categories of simplicial abelian groups and simplicial sets.

We demonstrate that such spurious findings arise from both deterministic and stochastic spurious correlations generated by an underlying Markov blanket. Utilizing new 200 $\mu$m and 350 $\mu$m data from the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope (JCMT), we derived flux densities of 10.8 $\pm$ 0.6 Jy and 4.5 $\pm$ 0.3 Jy, respectively. These measurements indicate that G29.96+0.46 possesses a mass of approximately 18 solar masses and demonstrates an extremely high surface density of $\sim$ 10 solar masses per square arcsecond. The 6.2 GHz masers are located $\sim$ 1" away from the central source, whereas the 22 GHz masers originate from the immediate vicinity of the protostar. We propose that the 22 GHz masers are triggered by the powerful outflows and jets characteristic of massive protostars, while the 6.2 GHz masers likely arise in the high-density environments of circumstellar disks. Furthermore, the co-occurrence of these masers alongside the extreme physical conditions found in G29.96+0.46 suggests that this region is a prime location for identifying potential massive stars currently embedded within their natal clouds. The observational data and conclusions presented here are intended to assist in interpreting ATMM data for newly discovered G-type masers. G29.96+0.46 is a relatively unobserved region situated close to the Galactic Center, and its study offers significant value for refining our understanding of massive star formation.

These measurements were conducted using a setup composed of two scintillation detectors and two neutron moderators. The study employs a novel approach to analyze data from this hybrid instrumentation, combining direct detection signals from scintillators with moderated neutron flux data. This allows for a simultaneous fit of hadronic interaction models across several key observables, including the atmospheric depth of shower maximum, muon density, electron density, and the depth of the first hadronic interaction. The analysis focuses on proton-induced showers and applies both the QGSJETII-04 and EPOS1.3 models. Furthermore, the research determines the relative normalization between the proton and hadronic components of the primary spectrum. The findings indicate that both models require higher direct detection rates and lower hadronic interaction depths than currently predicted. Additionally, the results suggest that increasing the pion production cross-section in the hadronic component of the primary spectrum could help alleviate these discrepancies. Ultimately, the study concludes that data from this solar neutron telescope can constrain the degrees of freedom in hadronic interaction models relevant to extensive air showers.

While $H_K$ typically varies linearly with thickness, we observed an anomalous S-shaped dependence in specific samples. We attribute these deviations to a nonmonotonic change in the out-of-plane lattice parameter, which influences the local crystal field and consequently the electronic band structure. By analyzing the thickness-dependent $H_K$ through a $d$-band model, we developed a straightforward method to estimate the relative contributions of $d$-band anisotropy, $d$-band SOC, and $s$-$p$ band SOC. Furthermore, an analytical model was employed to elucidate the origin of the $H_K$ behavior and the resulting balance between $d$-band and $s$-$p$ band SOC. These findings offer valuable insights for understanding the thickness-dependent anisotropy of thin magnetic layers and provide a framework to investigate the interplay among anisotropy, lattice strain, and band structure. The thickness range where $d$- and $s$-band SOC compete may extend to several nanometers in thicker films or nanoscale structures, potentially explaining the atypical anisotropy thickness dependence frequently observed experimentally. Additionally, this approach provides a means to assess the relative strengths of $d$-band and $s$-$p$ band SOC in magnetic layers.

While prior research has developed detection methods based on linguistic and structural data, this study introduces a novel perspective by analyzing the temporal evolution of fake news. We collected over 10,000 English-language fake and real stories from Reddit, tracking their popularity dynamics via comment counts. Our analysis reveals that the popularity curves of fake and real news are statistically indistinguishable, yet they differ fundamentally in their underlying temporal structures. Specifically, we demonstrate that fake news follows a dual power law distribution, whereas real news adheres to a single power law. These findings highlight that the rate at which news stories gain and lose popularity is a critical factor in distinguishing authenticity. This approach represents a new direction in fake news analysis, offering insights that complement existing methods by incorporating temporal dynamics. We also developed a classifier leveraging these differences in popularity evolution, which achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.81 on a test set. This result surpasses a baseline classifier trained solely on textual and structural features, confirming the discriminative power of our proposed features. Furthermore, we show that a model trained on Reddit data generalizes effectively to news stories from other sources, such as Twitter and TAP (Today I Learned) articles. We discuss the broader implications of these results and suggest potential applications, including the development of systems capable of identifying and removing fake news in real time. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/NoamShaked/RealVsFake.

This study focuses on constructing GCMs of odd order $n=4m+1$ with parameter $k=2m+1$, which are particularly valuable for optical applications and CAZAC sequence generation. This study employs ab initio calculations to examine local tunneling microscopy (LTM) images of individual Au adatoms on Si(111)-$(\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3})$-Ag surfaces. Complex systems are defined by extensive networks of components characterized by straightforward interactions and specific organizing rules, which give rise to their inherent complexity and capacity for self-organized criticality (SOC). These features are central to the study of complex systems theory and statistical physics. Lattice models, which represent systems through spatial arrangements of interacting components, serve as a primary framework for investigating such phenomena. Among the various processes defined on these structures, the "contact process" is a foundational model for understanding complex behavior and SOC in self-driven systems. This process was initially developed to describe phase separation in adsorbed binary mixtures and has since been recognized as a prototypical system for studying SOC. Despite its significance, previous investigations have been limited to low dimensions ($d=1$ and $d=2$). Although the system's parameters and fluctuations were examined numerically, no prior work provided an exact analysis of the contact process's statistical properties, its simplified variants, or their relationship to Behenna-SOC. Consequently, this paper begins with an examination of the contact process in dimensions $d=1,2,3$, offering an exact analysis

These frameworks generalize several well-established Markov decision processes, including an infinite version of the tabular problem featuring i.i.d. transitions, as well as continuous state and space problems governed by Lipschitz transition dynamics. The primary objective of this work is to establish the existence of stationary optimal policies within these infinite settings. To achieve this, we develop a novel approach that integrates a new iterative method—distinct from standard value and policy iteration schemes—with finite horizon approximation techniques. Notably, this process necessitates resolving a related infinite system of linear equations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that when valuations are discrete, the sequence of multipliers arising in this system converges to a specific irreducible sub-stochastic matrix associated with the decision problem under investigation. This matrix facilitates the derivation of robust bounds for the vector of states, thereby enabling the finite approximation of the original infinite system of linear equations. Under conditions where these bounds are sufficiently close, a stationary optimal policy can be identified within a prescribed neighborhood of the associated decision points. The algorithm presented here is applicable to state-space problems where transition dynamics are quantized into a finite number of distinct valuations. The algorithm is also adaptable to continuous state and space decision problems, provided an appropriate approximation of the Lipschitz dynamic functions is implemented. The algorithm's efficacy is validated through various state-space stochastic shortest path problems, with a particular emphasis on a continuous state and space decision problem featuring sinusoidal dynamic functions. The implementation relies on the E-TRIS software package. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ItamarGross/stochastic_shortest_paths_infinite. This study employed next-generation RNA sequencing to examine gene expression changes in the neocortex surrounding acute (24 hours) and chronic (14 days) lesions in juvenile rat brains. **1. Introduction**

Analyzing categorical data is essential across numerous fields, including biology, psychology, and social sciences. However, working with high-dimensional categorical data presents significant challenges. A primary obstacle is the difficulty in selecting appropriate models for analysis. For instance, one-dimensional high-dimensional data often leads to selection tasks where the goal is to identify important features (levels) from which feature selection or dimensionality reduction techniques can be applied. In contrast, multi-dimensional high-dimensional data typically involves constructing interaction models with a vast number of potential interactions that exceed the sample size. In all such scenarios, the core challenge lies in ensuring that the estimated models are both sparse and interpretable.

**1.1 Motivation**

One-dimensional categorical data are commonly encoded as dummy variables, where each level of a factor becomes a separate variable. While this representation is intuitive, it frequently results in a high-dimensional setting where the count of dummy variables surpasses the sample size $n$. Likelihood (ML) decoding to refine signal estimates is a common practice in various fields, including communications, radar, and navigation. However, deploying neural network-based RL agents in practical settings is challenging due to their "black box" characteristics, which hinder trustworthiness, and their high data requirements for training, which compromise real-time performance. This paper investigates the feasibility of applying these agents to phase estimation in orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems overawarand channel conditions. We introduce a novel exploration strategy that streamlines the policy network by eliminating the need for an observation layer, thereby accelerating both inference and training phases. This approach ensures that the finalized network relies solely on decoded subcarrier symbols rather than the received signal for inference, making it suitable for real-time applications. Furthermore, we enhance training efficiency by utilizing a batched data processing technique that fully exploits GPU parallelism. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a comparable mean square error (MSE) to existing solutions while reducing the network size by 66.67%, accelerating the inference speed by 1.85 times, and improving training speed by 1.4 times.

To address this, we introduce TruMongo, the inaugural flexible validation tool for MongoDB. TruMongo enables the definition of a unified validation schema applicable to an entire document population. Unlike previous approaches, TruMongo offers a rich set of constraints that can be expressed using a high-level, SQL-like language. We conducted a comprehensive benchmark comparing TruMongo against existing validation approaches, demonstrating that TruMongo exceeds the validation capabilities of prior work. Furthermore, we show how TruMongo facilitates consistent data cleaning across a population of similar documents, a task that was previously unachievable. Finally, we present an evaluation of the performance and scalability of TruMongo when processing large-scale datasets. The source code for TruMongo is available at https://github.com/NoamShaked/TrueMongo. MongoDB is open-source and can be accessed at https://www.mongodb.com/products/platform.

is examined within the framework of general relativity, where matter is modeled as an ideal fluid with barotropic equations of state, $p=\gamma\rho c^2$. It is demonstrated that, contrary to expectations, the leading edge of the high-Mach-number shock front does not traverse at the speed of light ($c$). Instead, for supersonic shocks, the tip velocity is determined by the local sound speed and the pressure gradient immediately behind the shock, resulting in a propagation speed strictly less than $c$. This finding contrasts with the behavior observed in Newtonian fluids, where the tip velocity equals the sound speed. While the shock's curvature causes the front to expand spherically, the fact that the tip moves slower than the sound speed implies a non-spherical expansion of high-pressure, high-density regions. Consequently, the high-pressure zone takes on an ellipsoidal shape, with the sound speed governing expansion along the polar axis and shock-velocity determining expansion along the equatorial direction. Numerical simulations of a strong explosion in static spacetime are conducted to validate these findings and determine the temporal evolution of the explosion radius. Furthermore, these results are compared with gravitational explosions occurring in both matter-dominated and de Sitter spacetimes. The paper concludes with an analysis of the flow structure across various regimes, including the sonic point, gravitational collapse leading to black hole formation, and the Taylor–Proudman effect. These findings hold relevance for gravitational explosions, supernova and gamma-ray burst outflows, astrophysical and laboratory explosions, volcanic eruptions, and the expansion of high-pressure regions in condensed matter physics.

Large Hadron Collider (LHC) initiated a high-luminosity upgrade, with plans to resume operations in 2027. This upgrade involves a tenfold increase in beam intensity and a significant enhancement in luminosity monitoring capabilities. A critical component of this enhancement is the development of a novel transverse feedback system designed to mitigate low-frequency beam instabilities during high-intensity fills. This paper presents the findings from a 2016 loss-of-proton experiment conducted at the LHC's Interaction Region 1 (IR1) aperture. The experiment involved equipping the LHC with a model of the new feedback system to validate its design through the observation of previously unseen proton instability modes. The results P-9000 and the system model are accessible at https://home.web.cern.ch/sites/new-cbns-feedback/home/simulations-and-models/loss-of-proton-expo.

Protons circulating in the LHC can develop various transverse feedback-driven instabilities, including the mode-coupling instability (MCI) and the coupled-bunch instability (CBI). The CBI was first detected during a loss-of-proton (LoP) experiment in 2016 by varying the spacing of high-current bunches to create a range of coupling impedances along the accelerator. This allowed for the identification of two previously unidentified CBI modes, designated as low-frequency CBI (LFCBI) and high-frequency CBI (HFCBI). The LFCBI was characterized by a narrow azimuthal distribution of affected bunches and a strong correlation between its growth rate and the total impedance of a specific impedance bucket (IB) along the ring. Conversely, the HFCBI exhibited a uniform azimuthal distribution, a weaker dependence on individual IB impedance, and a stronger dependence on the total ring impedance. These characteristics indicate that the LFCBI arises from a single dominant IB, while the HFCBI results from the coupling of all bunches to the aggregate impedance of the ring.

The MCI was identified by gradually increasing the current within individual bunches, thereby altering the impedance landscape along the LHC. This approach revealed a third instability, termed local-MCI (Local-MCI), which was characterized by a narrow azimuthal distribution of unstable bunches and a strong correlation with the impedance of a specific IB. The Local-MCI was attributed to the third harmonic cavity (3HC) in interaction region 5 (IR5).

background (CMB) serves as a primary method for constraining fundamental cosmological parameters. However, astrophysical point sources (PSs) represent a significant contaminant for current and future high-sensitivity experiments. This paper introduces a novel approach to estimate and mitigate CMB contamination from radio PSs. We collected a catalog of 1,015 very long baseline interferometry (VLBI)-monitored quasars from the VLBA 1.6 GHz catalog. For each source, we determined its position and flux density at C-band (5.9–7.6 GHz) using the GLEAM catalog and the ATCA 21cm Imaging Pipeline. We then fitted the multi-frequency data from all sources simultaneously with a power law model to derive individual spectral indices. By identifying the 10% of sources with the lowest root-mean-square (RMS) residuals between observed and fitted flux densities, we constructed a clean sub-mm point source catalog. Applying Bayesian inference, we calculated the angular size, surface brightness, and flux density distributions of these sources based on the median spectral indices of the low-RMS subset. Finally, we removed the effects of these sub-mm PSs from the ATCA 12-m 9 GHz CMB map, achieving a reduction in RMS contamination from 1.30 to 1.08 mK within a 10 arcmin circular region centered on 3C 273. To further lower contamination levels, future surveys require deeper observations across broader frequency bands with improved instrumental sensitivity. Additionally, employing multiple non-redundant baselines to precisely determine the positions and flux densities of radio PSs will be essential. These findings will assist in selecting QSOs for VLBI observations and aid in minimizing CMB contamination in future experiments.

the German physicist Max Born first interpreted the square of the wave function, $|\psi|^2$, as a probability density. This interpretation became a cornerstone of the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics, which remains the standard framework for understanding quantum phenomena. However, the Copenhagen approach has faced persistent criticism, and recently, it has encountered a significant challenge from the recently discovered de Broglie-Bohm (dBB) theory, or pilot wave theory. This theory offers a deterministic and realist alternative to quantum mechanics. Notably, both interpretations yield identical predictions in conventional laboratory settings. Nevertheless, a recent proposal suggests that when two laboratories share overlapping regions, exchanging their individual measurements of a single particle in that region could reveal the influence of distant events on local outcomes—a phenomenon known as "spooky action at a distance." This effect would directly contradict the local causality inherent in dBB theory. While the proposal has been implemented in systems involving multiple particles, we argue that it can also be achieved with a single particle by utilizing the ability to generate multiple de Broglie-Bohm trajectories for one particle in overlapping laboratory regions. Such a scenario would demonstrate that the path taken by a single particle is determined by distant events, thereby confirming the non-locality of dBB theory and Born's quantum mechanics. Furthermore, this effect would provide the first direct observation of the non-locality inherent in pilot wave theory. We further show that this phenomenon can be demonstrated through interference patterns in a double-slit experiment, where the presence of a detector at one slit alters the interference pattern observed at a distant screen. This result indicates that the particle detected on the screen was guided by a pilot wave originating from the region of the observed slit, a conclusion that cannot be accounted for if the particle were solely located within the Copenhagen probability cloud. Additionally, we present a theoretical experiment involving two entangled particles in separate laboratories, where the detection of one particle enables the "instantaneous" opening of a quantum Jarysch-Teller (J-T) channel for the other, illustrating how distant events can influence the behavior of a particle in a different location. These findings collectively highlight the profound non-locality of de Broglie-Bohm theory and the capacity to "instantaneously" establish communication channels between distant points using a single particle. Ultimately, these effects serve as clear manifestations of non-locality in both pilot wave theory and standard quantum mechanics, challenging the classical notion that physical influences cannot propagate faster than light. This approach allows us to incorporate the leading-order effects of general holographic operators composed of bulk scalar fields $\phi$ and their conjugate momenta $p_\phi$. Our findings indicate that the coefficient of $\delta\Delta$ is positive for both the DNV-TR and DNV-RTA cases, suggesting that these operators behave as relevant deformations, contrary to the usual expectation that UV operators are irrelevant. Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models are frequently employed to identify and classify human activities. However, these conventional approaches process raw data sequentially or in fixed windows, failing to leverage the spatial relationships inherent in the data. This limitation often results in suboptimal performance. This paper introduces a hybrid approach that integrates spatial features into these models, utilizing a 1D convolutional layer to extract activity-related features from raw acceleration and angular velocity sensor data. A linear layer then generates a class-specific embedding for each sample, which is subsequently processed by the LSTM network to produce the final prediction. Experimental results across multiple public datasets demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms existing techniques, offering superior performance at both activity-level and session-level classifications. The findings indicate that incorporating spatial features into CNN architectures significantly enhances prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the model's source code is available at https://github.com/ahmedsharshar99/CS-LSTM.

This study presents the results of a new, automated analysis of a sample of 2,000 flares from a single star, HD 269470. We measured key characteristics including flux, duration, rise and decay times, and colour indices. The duration distribution follows a power law with a slope of -1.5 for flares shorter than 10 minutes, which is longer than the typical 3-minute exposure time. On average, the decay time is six times greater than the rise time. The sample exhibits a significant excess of short-duration, low-amplitude flares, likely caused by instrumental effects or cosmic rays. We observed that flare properties vary with wavelength, with white-light flares being broader in H$\alpha$ and UV than in optical bands. Based on these findings, we conclude that the majority of white-light flares from solar-type stars are not driven by magnetic recombination events typical of solar flares. Instead, they resemble the "supergranule" transients seen in Ca II K images on the Sun, suggesting they may arise from magnetic activity at the boundaries of supergranules. HD 269470 displays a higher level of magnetic activity, as indicated by its frequent and intense flares, compared to Kepler-442 and Kepler-438. We provide the raw data and diagnostic images from our automated pipeline at http://www.astro.univ-lille.fr/~verner/keplerflare/. These data will be incorporated into a larger analysis of HD 269470, which includes a determination of the mass and radius of its transiting planet, HD 269470b.

transfer of life between planetary systems—has been discussed for over a century, its feasibility remains constrained by three primary factors: the velocity required to reach other stars, the durability of organisms during ejection and transit, and the probability of successful implantation and replication within a target system. While space agencies are now evaluating the first two factors through technological development and empirical testing, this study concentrates exclusively on the third challenge. We examine the conditions necessary for life to emerge, survive, and proliferate within planetary-mass bodies orbiting other stars, effectively functioning as seeds. Specifically, we analyze the habitability of such seeds across their formation, migration, and long-term evolution, covering timescales from 1 to 10 million years. Our results indicate that meteorite-sized seeds are unlikely to support the full lifecycle of life; they probably cannot generate ab initio life, retain implanted life, or sustain biospheres over millions of years. However, larger seeds are not only theoretically viable but also appear to be common. These substantial objects can acquire and nurture life from protoplanetary disks, retain it throughout migration, and maintain biospheres until they settle into the habitable zones of their parent stars. We characterize the properties and migration dynamics of these potential seeds, offering rough estimates of their abundance and expected numbers within the solar system. Ultimately, we conclude that larger meteorites and planetesimals are indeed capable of serving as effective seeds for interstellar life dispersal. Furthermore, comparing the lifespans of seeds and organisms on them to the interval between the emergence of life on habitable planets suggests a lower bound for the frequency of interstellar panspermia events, which we estimate to occur at least once every 100 million years. This rate exceeds the frequency of mass extinction events on Earth, implying that life on our planet may have originated one or more times from interstellar seeds. We discuss the testability of our hypotheses and highlight the significance of future missions designed to explore the origins of life on Earth and the reality of interstellar panspermia.

This paper introduces a short-horizon model-predictive controller designed to optimize a limited number of vehicles at specific locations, such as those equipped with onboard controllers for automated driving. This approach addresses a key limitation of conventional methods like splines and shock-tube models, which manage traffic over broad areas but lack the precision needed for individual vehicles. Unlike other high-fidelity strategies, such as spatially and temporally discretized methods and Karaman's method \cite{karaman2013optimization}, which achieve exact solutions within a grid resolution but require extensive computation, the proposed controller achieves computational complexity comparable to low-fidelity methods. Specifically, the computational effort scales linearly with the number of vehicles to be optimized rather than the geographic area they occupy. To ensure robustness against model inaccuracies and noisy observations, the controller integrates a particle filter representing the overall traffic network and employs a receding-horizon control strategy. Simulation results involving a platoon of cars on a freeway segment demonstrate the controller's ability to maintain desired performance metrics, such as spacing and speed, while remaining computationally efficient. Additionally, a simulation of a more realistic scenario featuring a mix of automated and human-driven vehicles validates the approach's scalability. Finally, a co-design algorithm is proposed to optimize the spatial grid resolution, balancing the accuracy of the predicted plan with computational demands. Keywords: Traffic state estimation, model-predictive control, particle filters, platoon control. \textit{Note: This work was presented at the American Control Conference 2019.}

This study demonstrates that failing to satisfy these constraints leads to unphysical behaviors, such as the generation of spurious gravitational radiation. We provide explicit calculations of asymptotic constraints for binary black hole systems in isolation and within gauge fields. Furthermore, we show that these issues can be mitigated by imposing no-falling boundary conditions on the canonical momentum $\pi^{\phi}$ of any non-gravitationally interacting sector, a requirement that goes beyond standard BSSN boundary conditions. These findings have significant implications for long-term simulations of binary mergers and the analysis of residual data at infinity. If boundary conditions at large distances are not sufficiently rigorous, the extraction of gravitational wave amplitudes and phase information may be compromised by unphysical spectral components originating from the source. Consequently, this could hinder the accurate identification of subtle physical effects, such as memory terms or nonlinearities arising from the interaction between gravitational waves and the background curvature generated by the binary system. While increasing the number of grid points at infinity can reduce the magnitude of these effects, it cannot eliminate them entirely. We conclude that to achieve the precision required for extracting small post-Newtonian corrections from merger data, boundary conditions at spatial infinity must be strengthened. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that no-falling conditions are necessary at spatial infinity for simulations involving non-gravitationally interacting sectors, a requirement that exceeds the standard no-inflow conditions typically employed. Finally, we offer recommendations for future simulations, including the use of absorbing boundary conditions at spatial infinity to eliminate no-falling conditions in simulations with periodic boundary conditions in the $z$-direction.

alous Hall effect in magnetic materials has heightened the significance of the topological anomalous Hall effect. This phenomenon arises when a finite anomalous Hall conductance, generated by the Berry curvature of a band with non-zero Chern number, scatters charge carriers. We demonstrate that this topological character can be manipulated by altering the Berry curvature of the electronic bands. Specifically, in ferromagnetic thin films exhibiting the anomalous Hall effect, we achieve this control by modifying the shape of the Berry curvature in the k-space occupied by the carriers. This approach is accomplished by tuning the magnetic anisotropy through in-plane magnetic fields, which vary the boundaries of the k-space region responsible for the anomalous Hall conductance. Consequently, the anomalous Hall conductance can be switched from a topological to a conventional state, or vice versa, by changing the direction of magnetization relative to the easy axis. This mechanism relies on the non-conservation of the Berry curvature within the occupied k-space and the topological nature of the anomalous conductance. The validity of this model is confirmed by quantitative calculations based on first-principles band structures of selected magnetic thin films. The ability to switch the type of the anomalous Hall effect via in-plane magnetic fields is particularly valuable for applications involving current-induced magnetization dynamics, such as magnetoresistive random access memory.

Similarly, currencies such as the Japanese Yen or the US Dollar are valuable because they are produced by their respective governments, entities that are extremely difficult to emulate. Consequently, assets and money possess value due to their "uniqueness" and "unimitability." This analogy also elucidates economic phenomena such as inflation, deflation, and stock market crashes. Additionally, it offers a justification for the existence of large corporations and various other phenomena within the realms of biology, chemistry, and sociology. Ultimately, this analogy provides a cohesive explanation for the origins and behaviors of both individuals and society. This paper details the justification for the existence of individuals, societies, money, assets, and their respective values, as well as the dynamics governing their dynamics, thereby offering a comprehensive explanation for the emergence of life and a unified framework for understanding the entire universe. This proposal is intended to serve as a robust foundation for future research in biology, artificial intelligence, economics, and related disciplines.

While many species rely on vision to select locations and guide motion, blind species like nematodes must instead depend on sensory input from their environment to achieve these goals. This study focuses on how *Caenorhabditis elegans* utilize oxygen to locate food and traverse chemical gradients. We tracked large populations of this organism while they foraged in environments with varying food and oxygen levels. Our analysis reveals that *C. elegans* can identify bacterial food through oxygen alone, adjusting their preferred setpoints based on food availability. This research offers insights into how sensory-driven organisms like *C. elegans* process information to locate resources and follow chemical trails, and it provides a framework for investigating how other blind animals adapt to spatial variations in environmental factors such as temperature, humidity, and carbon dioxide.

**Introduction**

Reconstructing visible and occluded surfaces from a single 2D image is crucial for applications such as autonomous driving, virtual/augmented reality, and film production. While significant progress has been made in occluded surface reconstruction using deep learning [2–4], most existing methods [2, 3] are limited to scenarios involving total transparency (e.g., glass). Consequently, they often fail to accurately recover partially or fully occluded objects in real-world settings. This paper focuses on addressing the reconstruction of occluded surfaces from a solitary 2D image given partially or totally transparent objects.

**Related Work**

Recent years have seen a surge in research on deep learning-based methods for reconstructing occluded surfaces from a single 2D image. These approaches generally fall into two categories: implicit and explicit methods.

**Implicit Methods**

Implicit methods [5–10] typically represent transparent objects as glass and rely on novel view synthesis to infer occluded areas. For example, Wu et al. [6] developed a two-stage pipeline: first generating a novel view without transparency, then blending it with the original image to create the final rendered image. However, these methods often struggle with accurate depth estimation and may produce artifacts in the occluded regions.

Unlike traditional methods such as Verlet or leapfrog, which are limited by the smallest timestep required to resolve high-frequency harmonic oscillations—often resulting in a timestep 10 to 100 times smaller than necessary for sampling slow degrees of freedom and incurring significant computational costs due to excessive integration steps—MTSA utilizes different timesteps for variables ranging from constrained to nearly free. The proposed method, named multiple-timestep constraint algorithm (MTCA), is a multiple-time-step force decomposition scheme that combines the efficiency of Verlet integration with the advantages of Leimkuhler and Skeel's reversible integrator. By employing a hierarchy of timesteps based on constraint levels, from fully constrained to unconstrained degrees of freedom, MTCA achieves computational efficiency comparable to Verlet integration while maintaining the high acceptance rates characteristic of reversible integrators. Numerical experiments on various molecular models confirm that the algorithm's computational cost per step is comparable to Verlet integration, its numerical accuracy is on par with SHAKE and LINCS constraints, and its high acceptance rate significantly reduces the computational cost per sampled configuration compared to standard integrators. Annealing involves slowly varying control parameters to navigate between phases, whereas quenches entail sudden changes to control parameters or interactions, causing the system to become trapped in a dynamical mismatch between its state and the new equilibrium. In this study, we investigate the thermalization of the one-dimensional transverse Ising model following both quantum and classical transitions across the critical point. We demonstrate that, unlike the case of a sudden change in the interaction parameter, neither the quantum nor the classical critical point acts as a dynamical phase transition when viewed through the lens of average thermalization time. Instead, the system exhibits non-ergodic behavior, failing to fully equilibrate even for relatively short times after the transition. Specifically, the average thermalization time diverges precisely at the critical point for both types of transitions. Additionally, we observe a secondary divergence in thermalization time at a specific value below the true critical point, which we attribute to the emergence of a dynamical phase. This secondary divergence aligns with predictions from the theory of quantum quenching regarding dominant eigenvalues. Additionally, we identify a secondary indication of criticality in the structure of spin correlations, which we term a dynamical critical exponent. Finally, we note that these secondary indications of criticality have been reported in other systems as well. We conclude by suggesting potential applications of these findings in detecting phase transitions using the one-dimensional Truncated Ising Model.

**Introduction**

Intelligent systems are increasingly embedded in daily life, from automated teller machines to self-driving cars. This trend is driven by the ability of machine learning models to enhance performance through scale—specifically, by training on larger datasets and updating with more data. However, the reliance on data also creates a vulnerability: datasets contain sensitive personal information that could be stolen. Although data leakage via traditional methods is well-documented, this paper focuses on a less explored area: using machine learning models to leak training data during the training phase.

Neural networks have achieved remarkable success in tasks like image classification and natural language processing. A key factor in this success is the scale of data and models. For instance, Google's Language Model 1 has billions of parameters and was trained on vast text corpora. Similarly, GPT-3 was trained on 300 gigabytes of text data and 210 million images. As models grow in size, so does the potential for privacy violations. light propagation within the weak-field approximation of general relativity. This process involves solving the null geodesic equation, which determines how photons traverse gravitational fields. While the weak-field geodesic equation offers a perturbative method for finding high-precision astrometric positions, it requires initial conditions at both the observer and the source, making it a boundary value problem. In contrast, the standard approach for practical high-precision astrometry involves a two-step method: first estimating the observer's position using the inverse scattering equation, and second, determining the source position via the initial value problem, which applies the high-precision weak-field geodesic equation. This paper demonstrates that the inverse scattering equation can itself be formulated as a weak-field geodesic equation, enabling a direct determination of high-precision astrometric positions in a single step. By employing the light-cone gauge, we derive an analytical expression for the inverse scattering equation that eliminates the need for iterative numerical solutions. Furthermore, this expression allows for the direct calculation of high-precision positions of sources such as quasars and Gaia catalog stars from their nominal positions and observed arrival directions. We validate this single-step method through numerical examples and confirm its efficacy by applying it to actual data from the VLBA and the Gaia mission. Additionally, we provide a concise overview of alternative geodesic equation formulations and their corresponding positions, along with a summary of relevant prior literature. The findings indicate that the light-cone gauge serves as an efficient computational tool for high-precision astrometry, offering a straightforward solution to the inverse scattering equation without numerical iteration. Consequently, both the observer position estimation and source position estimation can be executed as single-step calculations without numerical integration of the geodesic equation. These results facilitate the development of a highly efficient algorithm for astrometry, which can be readily implemented in existing codes for positional corrections or in ray-tracing simulations of light propagation in strong gravitational fields.

This paper examines the convergence properties of the posterior distribution $\hat{\pi}(\theta|y)$ associated with a Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) $\hat{\theta}(y)$ in Bayesian inference. Specifically, we demonstrate that if the mapping $\theta \mapsto y(\theta)$ is twice differentiable and the matrix $A(\theta) = \mathbb{E}[y(y|\theta)y(y|\theta)^T]$ is non-singular, then the posterior distribution of the Bayesian estimator $\hat{\theta}(y)$ converges to a Gaussian distribution as the sample size $n$ approaches infinity. Furthermore, we show that these findings extend to cases where $y(\theta)$ is non-differentiable, provided certain conditions on the eigenvalues of $A(\theta)$ are met. SMT solver MathSAT was introduced by De Moura in 2009. However, MathSAT does not currently support this format. Instead, users are expected to utilize the "TRP" extension, which was first implemented by Piskac in 2010. This paper presents the second iteration of the proof format, outlining its design objectives and potential applications. Additionally, it details how proof checkers can leverage this format to validate proofs generated by various solvers, and how human users can work with these proofs using the Prover9 theorem prover. The TRP format extends beyond mere verification; it encapsulates all necessary information regarding the proof's internal structure, generated lemmas, and applicable inference rules. As a result, it serves as a comprehensive record of the proof process, enabling users to reconstruct the proof step-by-step within Prover9. This reconstruction allows for the identification of lemmas that are equivalent to the original proof, thereby facilitating the generation of new, simpler proofs. Furthermore, the format includes metadata regarding solver options and parameters, allowing for the precise replication of the conditions under which a specific proof was created. The proposed format is backward compatible with the previous version and represents a significant advancement over the TRP format by providing all essential details required to reconstruct proofs in any supported CNF-independent intermediate format. Consequently, it can be utilized as a complete log format for proofs generated by modern solvers. We have implemented a Prolog-based proof checker that validates all aspects of the format and aids in reconstructing proofs step-by-step. This checker is accessible at http://www.cs.cas.cz/~dvorak/proof-checker/. Finally, we present experimental results from reconstructing proofs using our checker, along with evaluations of proofs generated by the STP solver. The TRP2 format is intended as an intermediate solution until a new standard is established; the eventual goal is a format that is both solver- and proof-checker-independent. Such a standard would allow for the preservation of all relevant information regarding proofs, their generation processes, and equivalence, without being constrained by the specific algorithms or decisions of any single solver. Ultimately, this would enhance the transparency of automated reasoning and improve the understandability of generated proofs.

In this paper, we utilize Bell's inequality to analyze the debate between Einstein and Bohr, highlighting how their positions align with local and nonlocal hidden variable theories, respectively. Furthermore, by applying General Relativity to Bell's inequality, we show that a collapsing star can prevent the detection of nonlocality. This implies that if macroscopic objects were to violate Bell's inequality, it would suggest that General Relativity is invalid. Consequently, the failure of such nonlocality at the macroscopic level offers a pathway to determine the scale where quantum mechanics transitions into classical physics. (Published as part of the Proceedings of the XI Latin American School on Cosmology and Gravitation, held in Buenos Aires, Argentina, October 2019.)

Internet of Things (IoT) technologies has generated substantial potential for societal advancement, it has also triggered significant security concerns. The widespread deployment of AI and IoT devices has exacerbated vulnerabilities within information systems, making them attractive targets for malicious actors. To address these challenges, this study introduces the AI-IoT framework, which combines advanced algorithms with networked smart devices. Furthermore, we examine various cyber threats and attacks, including ransomware, malware, phishing, and denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, that jeopardize the safety of this framework. Finally, we propose security measures and strategies designed to protect the AI-IoT framework from these dangers. This research offers insights into the vulnerabilities of the AI-IoT ecosystem and provides actionable recommendations for enhancing its security posture. The proposed security solutions are particularly relevant for government agencies, law enforcement, and other public sector entities responsible for safeguarding critical infrastructure. By mitigating risks associated with AI and IoT adoption, this work supports the secure development and deployment of these transformative technologies. To maximize the benefits of AI-IoT while minimizing potential threats, stakeholders must implement the security protocols outlined in this paper. Additionally, researchers, academicians, and industry professionals are encouraged to further explore these topics and apply the proposed solutions to ensure the resilience of AI-IoT systems.

This research presents new time-resolved optical spectra covering the entire visible spectrum, recorded during the outburst of 2011 January 29--February 1. The findings indicate that V392 Per's outbursts exhibit characteristics typical of classical novae, including high optical luminosity, strong emission lines, and a spectrum resembling that of a hydrogen-rich (AM) subtype. The measured accretion disk temperature aligns with expectations for high-mass systems. Furthermore, the spectral energy distribution and line profiles suggest an intrinsic optical luminosity of approximately $10^{39}$--$10^{40}$~erg~s$^{-1}$, which is consistent with the upper limits of classical nova outbursts. The analysis of the time evolution of the spectrum and line profiles reveals a prolonged period of nova-like behavior, a feature uncommon in other known high-mass AM novae. Additionally, the optical variability of the 2011 outburst was found to be more complex than previously observed in this system. While the event was classified as a classical nova, the extreme luminosity and intricate nature of the optical variability imply that further investigation is required to fully comprehend the physics of such outbursts in high-mass X-ray binaries. The complete dataset will serve as a valuable asset for refining the evolutionary models of AM novae. The 2011 outburst of V392 Per was detected by the Swift/UVOT instrument, and the resulting images are available for download. The objective is to achieve a feedback rate of $O(\log_2 N_r)$ bits, ensuring the encoder conveys information at $\Omega(\log_2 N_r)$ bits per channel realization to maximize system performance. Specifically, the codebook entries are defined by independent power law fractional Brownian motion (fBm) processes. Feedback decoding is achieved via collaborative dictionary learning (CDD). Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed method attains near-optimal rate-distortion curves compared to existing codebooks and effectively adapts to varying channel conditions. To our knowledge, this represents the initial instance of utilizing self-similar fBm processes for codebook creation. The key contributions are detailed as follows: (i) To attain a feedback rate of $O(\log_2 N_r)$ bits, the feedback precoder rate-distortion problem is reformulated so that the mean-square error (MSE) between the optimal low-rank decomposition and its Bayesian estimate remains bounded; (ii) the combined uplink feedback power and codebook dimension are shown to directly influence the feedback rate-distortion performance, with the proposed power allocation policy ensuring the feedback precoder rate-distortion problem attains an $O(\log_2 N_r)$ feedback rate; (iii) the feedback precoder behaves as an independent power law fBm process, enabling the application of asymptotic analysis to derive a closed-form solution for the optimal low-rank decomposition; (iv) the CDD algorithm is employed to reduce complexity in feedback decoding, and (v) simulations confirm that the feedback rate-distortion problem is solved optimally, the CDD scheme adapts to different channel conditions, and the overall system performance is near-optimal.

In this study, we present a molecular dynamics simulation of a dry, square-lattice, coarse-grained monolayer lipid model under an imposed temperature gradient. The simulation reveals a robust 2D Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff (BCH) crosscurrent: the lipid phase separation induced by the temperature gradient shifts the phase boundary caused by an external affinity field, a phenomenon that persists even when thermal or affinity fluctuations are present. We introduce a generalization of the 1D BCH relation to two dimensions and derive a corresponding theoretical expression. This formula is validated against simulation data across various gradients of affinity and affinity field strengths, as well as for lipids with differing hydrophobic tail lengths. These findings suggest that BCH crosscurrents can be harnessed to manipulate the self-assembly of monolayer lipids into functional, spatially organized, and stable patterns on surfaces. To our knowledge, this represents the first demonstration of a robust, closed-loop heat current in a one-dimensional 2D monolayer liquid. We conclude by proposing a molecular-level coarse-grained model for lipids and outlining potential extensions of our current model.

The analysis demonstrates that the resulting compact bodies possess an underdense core characterized by a density lower than the halo's central density. These findings indicate that the final state of collapse is governed by dark matter rather than baryonic interactions. Specifically, we determined that the density contrast between the object and the ambient halo, expressed as $(\rho_{\rm obj}/\rho_{\rm halo})$, is given by $0.15\,(\sigma_{\rm vir}/20)\,(\Lambda/11.2)^2$, where $\sigma_{\rm vir}$ represents the virial overdensity and $\Lambda$ denotes the initial Jeans length in units of the halo's fundamental length scale. The measured object density is found to be slightly higher than the average density inside the halo, which is consistent with the condition $\rho_{\rm obj}/\rho_{\rm halo} = 3/\pi$ derived from the variational principle for a uniform sphere. We conclude that galaxy formation is driven by dark matter, and that the properties of galactic centers are determined by the initial conditions of gravitational collapse. These results provide a theoretical basis for the low-density cores observed in galactic dark matter profiles. (Figure: 4, Table: 1, Equation: 5, Reference: 63)

The objective is to enhance secrecy rate by leveraging a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) to generate distinct radiation beams for each user while directing power toward their respective locations to improve the secrecy capacity of the overall system. The problem is formulated as an optimization task designed to maximize the minimum individual secrecy rate among all users, subject to the constraints that the RIS must form exactly $K$ beams, with each beam aligned to a specific user. Due to the non-convex nature of the objective function and constraints, the solution was approached in two stages. First, assuming fixed phase shifts for the users, the power allocation for the information symbols was optimized to boost the sum secrecy rate of all users, solved via a successive convex approximation (SCA) method. Second, the phase shifts allocated to each user were successively optimized to maximize the sum secrecy rate, utilizing an alternating optimization algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that both proposed schemes significantly outperform existing methods. Additionally, two alternative schemes are introduced: one focuses on maximizing the sum of the $p$-th power of the users' individual secrecy rates, and the other aims to maximize the overall system's secrecy capacity, defined as the sum of rates guaranteed to all users. For these two schemes, solutions were derived in a closed form. Keywords: Physical layer security, multi-user downlink, reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS), sum secrecy rate, closed-form solution.

However, current methods often fail to capture the full complexity of natural language interactions. This study introduces a framework for automatically generating statements performed by virtual agents in text-based games and evaluates various models across different games to examine their ability to comprehend these statements. The proposed generation framework integrates a game engine, a citation-based evaluation system, and a new generation-based system that leverages large language models alongside external knowledge graphs. Furthermore, the paper addresses several existing limitations when evaluating agent performance in baseline games. Experimental results indicate that contemporary large language models achieve high levels of understanding, yet they still struggle with specific tasks, such as interpreting the meaning of pronouns. Text-based games are accessible, cost-effective, and scalable; by utilizing the automatic generation framework presented here, researchers can develop new evaluations that more accurately reflect the extent of an agent's natural language capabilities. This paper introduces a regularization technique that significantly reduces the number of LSTM parameters needed during training without compromising performance. The proposed method involves regularizing selected hidden states at specific time steps based on another state from a different step, effectively acting as a form of data augmentation that enhances the model's ability to generalize. This approach, which we term state alignment, is straightforward to implement and requires no extra computational power beyond standard training. Furthermore, it eliminates the need for hyperparameter search, as it does not involve tuning learning rates. We validate our approach on two classification tasks: predicting the next word in a sentence and sentiment analysis. In both cases, we achieve performance comparable to an equivalent model with double the parameter count, as well as a model twice as large. Additionally, we demonstrate that the benefits of state alignment persist even when the models are evaluated on unseen domains. Finally, we release the Python code for state alignment along with a dataset designed to generalize language models to new domains, which can be found at https://github.com/roberta12/state-alignment-lstm.

This paper argues that adopting such a formulation is unnecessarily restrictive. We propose a more general statement: for any set of states, the charge-to-mass ratio must not exceed a universal maximum that applies to representations that could be screened by those states. This generalized version does not reference specific irreducible representations and is therefore less constrained. We demonstrate that in $d=4$ gravity with abelian gauge fields, the standard conjecture follows from this broader framework when applied to states experiencing the Coulomb force, as their screening behavior is governed by the same bound. Additionally, in $d=4$ gravity with global symmetries, we present a related, potentially more fundamental, conjecture regarding the screening capability of states carrying global charges. We conclude by highlighting several promising extensions of this work, including applications to higher-dimensional field theories, theories with non-abelian gauge fields, and the search for a more fundamental underpinning of the conjecture itself.
